131.event_title: Jan Hus refuses to recant at the Council of Constance
131.event: The Czech priest and reformer Jan Hus travelled to the Council of Constance in 1414 expecting to explain his views, but he was imprisoned soon after he arrived. At his hearings in June 1415 he was presented with a list of teachings attributed to him and urged to recant in order to save his life; he refused, and maintained that he did not hold all of the teachings as charged. On 6 July 1415 the council condemned him as a heretic and handed him over to the secular authorities, who executed him by burning that same day.
131.explanation: Hus chose death over disowning what he believed, and his execution made him a lasting national and religious symbol in Bohemia and an inspiration to later reformers such as Martin Luther.
131.tie_back: The kural ranks right conduct above life itself, and Hus, offered his life in exchange for a recantation he considered false, guarded his integrity at the cost of his life.
131._accuracy_note: A very close fit for valuing conduct above life, though Hus's stand concerned religious conviction as much as personal conduct.

132.event_title: Boethius writes the Consolation of Philosophy in prison
132.event: Boethius, a Roman senator who had become Master of Offices, one of the most senior officials at the court of the Ostrogothic king Theoderic, fell out with others at court, was accused of treason and of practising magic, and was imprisoned and later executed. While awaiting death he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy, an imagined dialogue in prose and verse between the prisoner and a lady who personifies Philosophy. In it Philosophy distinguishes the goods of fortune, such as riches, status and power, from the true goods of virtue and wisdom, and argues that his fall had not taken from him the things of real worth.
132.explanation: Written by a man who had lost wealth, office and freedom, the book became one of the most widely read works of the Middle Ages and a classic statement that virtue is the one possession fortune cannot remove.
132.tie_back: Like the kural, Boethius weighed wealth, rank and power one by one and concluded that virtue alone remained a true companion when everything else was gone.
132._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's survey of alternatives ending in conduct as the only lasting support, though the book argues for virtue and wisdom together rather than conduct alone.

133.event_title: Narayana Guru consecrates a Shiva lingam at Aruvippuram
133.event: Narayana Guru, a sage and social reformer whose family belonged to the Ezhava community, then ranked low in the Hindu caste order, consecrated a stone taken from the Neyyar river as a Shiva lingam at Aruvippuram in 1888. At the time only Brahmin priests were allowed to install temple deities, so the act broke orthodox practice and was challenged by upper-caste critics who questioned his right to perform it. The shrine became the Aruvippuram Shiva temple, and Narayana Guru went on to found temples in southern India and Ceylon that welcomed people of all castes.
133.explanation: The consecration is regarded as a turning point in Kerala's social reform movement, because it asserted that spiritual authority comes from a person's life and learning rather than from the caste into which they are born.
133.tie_back: On the reading of modern commentators who take the kural as a critique of status by birth, Narayana Guru's act embodies its claim that conduct, not birth, is what makes a person noble.
133._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for the universal reading of the kural that conduct outranks birth, but the event is about challenging caste rules rather than a demonstration of personal conduct as such.

134.event_title: Francis Bacon falls from office for taking gifts from litigants
134.event: Francis Bacon, the philosopher and essayist who had been Lord Chancellor of England since 1618, was charged in Parliament in 1621 with accepting gifts from people whose cases were before him. He pleaded guilty, was heavily fined and sentenced to imprisonment in the Tower of London; the fine was later waived and he spent only a few days in the Tower, but he was never again allowed to sit in Parliament or hold political office. Bacon maintained that the gifts had not affected his judgments, and he devoted his remaining years to writing and philosophy.
134.explanation: The episode shows that even one of the most learned men of his age could not recover his public standing once his conduct in office was found wanting, while his intellectual work continued and grew.
134.tie_back: The kural says lost learning can be regained but a lapse in conduct ruins one's standing; Bacon's learning stayed with him and kept producing books, but his lapse ended his public career for good.
134._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the contrast between recoverable learning and unrecoverable loss of standing, although the kural speaks of a Brahmin's duties and some historians see Bacon's fall as partly factional.

135.event_title: Boris Onishchenko is disqualified for a rigged epee at the Montreal Olympics
135.event: During the fencing event of the modern pentathlon at the 1976 Olympic Games, the epee of the Soviet pentathlete Boris Onishchenko registered hits on opponents it did not appear to have touched. The British team asked for the weapon to be inspected, and it was found to have been modified so that it could register a hit even when none had been made. Onishchenko was disqualified, the Soviet team was eliminated, and Great Britain went on to win the team gold medal.
135.explanation: The case remains one of the most notorious acts of cheating in Olympic history, and it showed that a rise won by deceit can collapse in an instant once the means are exposed.
135.tie_back: The kural holds that true eminence never comes to a person without right conduct, just as prosperity never settles on the envious; Onishchenko's rigged weapon brought him not honour but lasting disgrace.
135._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it illustrates that rank cannot be gained without right conduct, but it does not touch the kural's analogy with envy.

136.event_title: Jackie Robinson promises Branch Rickey he will not retaliate
136.event: At a meeting in 1945, Brooklyn Dodgers executive Branch Rickey spent hours acting out the racial hostility Jackie Robinson would face as the first Black player in modern major league baseball, and told him he wanted a player with the courage not to fight back. Robinson, who by his own later account had believed in retaliation since childhood, promised that there would be no incident. When he joined the Dodgers in 1947 he endured abuse without striking back, and he went on to become one of the game's stars.
136.explanation: Robinson's self-control was a deliberate strategy: both men understood that a single angry incident could be used to halt the integration of the sport.
136.tie_back: The kural describes the strong-minded who never slacken because they know the harm a lapse would bring; Robinson held firm precisely because he understood what one lapse would cost.
136._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of firmness grounded in knowing the consequences of a lapse, though Robinson's restraint was a strategic promise for a cause as well as personal conduct.

137.event_title: South African cricket captain Hansie Cronje admits taking bookmakers' money
137.event: Hansie Cronje, captain of South Africa's national cricket team and one of the country's most admired sportsmen, was charged by Delhi police in April 2000 with fixing one-day matches played in India, which he at first denied. He was sacked as captain, and in testimony before the King Commission of inquiry in June 2000 he admitted taking money from bookmakers and offering teammates money to underperform. In October 2000 the United Cricket Board of South Africa banned him from cricket for life.
137.explanation: Cronje's fall was so striking because his reputation for leadership had been built on years of disciplined play, and it was undone by choices he had no need to make.
137.tie_back: The kural contrasts the eminence gained through conduct with the needless disgrace a lapse brings; Cronje rose through the first and fell through the second.
137._accuracy_note: A strong fit for the kural's paired outcomes of eminence and self-inflicted disgrace; this event is also used once elsewhere in the book.

138.event_title: Nicholas Winton's rescue of children from Czechoslovakia comes to light
138.place: Prague, Czechoslovakia, and London, United Kingdom
138.event: Nicholas Winton, a London stockbroker, went to Prague at the end of 1938 and, working with colleagues including Trevor Chadwick and Doreen Warriner, organised transports that brought 669 children, most of them Jewish, from Czechoslovakia to Britain in 1939. He said little about it for nearly fifty years, until his wife found his 1939 scrapbook of the children's names and photographs. In 1988 he appeared on the BBC programme That's Life!, where he was surprised to meet some of the people he had rescued, now adults.
138.explanation: A single season of good work in 1939 grew, unseen, into hundreds of lives and the families that followed them, and was recognised only decades later.
138.tie_back: The kural calls good conduct a seed from which good things grow; Winton's actions bore fruit long after they were done, in people he had not seen for half a century.
138._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of good conduct as a seed bearing lasting fruit, though it shows only the good half of the kural, not the sorrow that bad conduct brings.

139.event_title: The Chofetz Chaim publishes his code on the laws of harmful speech
139.event: In 1873 Rabbi Yisrael Meir Kagan, then about thirty-five and living in Radun, published a book that systematically set out the Jewish laws forbidding lashon hara, harmful speech about others, and gossip. The work, titled Chafetz Chaim, became the authoritative text on the ethics of speech, and its author became known everywhere by its name. He also wrote a companion ethical treatise on guarding the tongue, Shemirat HaLashon.
139.explanation: Kagan treated careful speech not as occasional politeness but as a discipline to be trained until it becomes habit, and his book still shapes Jewish teaching on speech.
139.tie_back: The kural says people of right conduct cannot speak evil even by a slip of the tongue; Kagan devoted his first book to building exactly that habituated guard over speech.
139._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the book teaches the discipline of speech the kural praises, but it is a work of instruction rather than an event showing that discipline under test.

140.event_title: Ignaz Semmelweis fails to win over his colleagues
140.event: In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis, a doctor at the maternity clinic of the Vienna General Hospital, required staff to wash their hands in a chlorinated lime solution before examining patients, and deaths from childbed fever fell sharply. Many colleagues rejected his explanation, partly because it implied that doctors themselves were carrying the disease to their patients. He set out his findings in a full book only in 1861, and after unfavourable reviews he answered his critics with harshly worded open letters; his doctrine was generally accepted only later.
140.explanation: Semmelweis was right on the science, yet his discovery saved far fewer lives in his own time than it might have, in part because he could not bring the medical world along with him.
140.tie_back: The kural says that those who cannot live in harmony with the world remain ignorant however much they have learned; Semmelweis's case shows how knowledge without the skill of persuading others can fail to do its good.
140._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it illustrates learning that failed to fit with the world, but much of the blame lay with his colleagues' resistance rather than with Semmelweis, and he was far from ignorant.
